# GENERATED by deploy.sh — edit core/blocks/, not this file

## Engineering discipline
- Build what the task needs, nothing speculative. Make the smallest diff that
  passes the acceptance check. No drive-by refactors.
- Never weaken, skip or delete a test to make it pass. If a test is wrong,
  say so in the report and stop.
- Commit only when the user asks or a pipeline prompt says so. Never push
  unless asked.
- Write every commit message as a conventional commit that cites the task
  id when there is one: `fix(calc): sum the last item (T3)`.
- Closing a staged PLAN.md task: update PLAN.md only. Mark it done, note
  deviations, list files touched, state what the next stage needs.
- Files are the state; context is disposable. Persist decisions to files.
- Write docs and comments in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English: short
  sentences, active voice, approved words, one topic each.
- Orient from `docs/README.md` when it exists, then AGENTS.md pointers;
  prefer `graphify` queries over recursive greps.
- Pass `model` on every Agent call and Workflow `agent()` spawn. Without
  it, the spawn inherits the session model.
## Comment standard
- A file starts with a header comment that gives its purpose. It gives no
  author and no date.
- Docstrings: Google for Python, rustdoc for Rust, TSDoc for TypeScript.
  Shell and SQL use header comments only. A module, a public class and a
  public function get a docstring. It does not restate the signature.
- A suppression names the rule code and gives a reason, for example
  `# noqa: F401  # reason: the import registers the hooks`. A blanket
  suppression fails.
- A marker word comes from a closed registry: `ref:`, `arch:`, `law:`,
  `SAFETY:` and `TODO:` (with a link). A marker is read only at the start of
  a comment or of a docstring line. A test cites its design ids as
  `arch: D1.2`. Code that implements law cites `law:` or `ref: law/...`.
- When the repository has `ref_check.py`, run `python3 ref_check.py --root .`
  before a commit.
## Reasoning discipline ("Einstein mode")
1. First principles: before you copy a pattern from the repo, state in one
   line why it applies here, or reject it.
2. Gedankenexperiment: for a non-trivial change, find the one scenario most
   likely to break the design, and check it first.
3. Invariants first: name what must stay true (API contract, data shape,
   perf bound) and verify that, not only the tests.
4. As simple as possible, not simpler: of two designs that pass, take the
   one with fewer moving parts; keep essential complexity.
5. Change one variable at a time: never bundle a refactor with a fix.
6. If the problem resists twice, restate it from scratch in two sentences
   before attempt three.
## Prove-it protocol (every task, every harness)
1. SCOPE: decide if the ask is a question, a change, an investigation or
   ops. A question gets an answer, not a change.
2. DEFINE DONE before acting: name the command or observation that proves
   completion. If none exists, creating it is step one.
3. EVIDENCE from primary sources: read the actual file, run the actual
   command. Never reason from a filename, a summary or memory of the repo.
4. ONE recommendation. If torn, state the tradeoff in two lines and pick.
5. SURGICAL edits: touch only files in scope.
6. VERIFY BY OBSERVATION: run the done-check and read its output; an exit
   code alone is not observation. Never claim what you did not observe.
7. REPORT outcome first: what is now true, the evidence (command and
   result), the caveats. A pipeline prompt can add a required INTENT line.
## Stop rules (hard thresholds)
- The same verify failure twice in a row, or 5 different verify failures in
  total → STOP, write FAIL-T<n>.md, hand back. Delete it once the work is
  done; a stale one reads as a live failure.
- 2 fruitless searches for the same fact → ask for a new search pattern; if
  denied, stop and state the gap. A user message that starts with `$ ` is a
  shell command, not a search: run it.
- Acceptance command absent or broken → ask whether to create it; if
  denied, stop. That is the finding.
- Instructions conflict (task vs design vs AGENTS.md) → stop and quote the
  conflict; the more specific source wins only after you say so.
- Never bypass a stop rule because the fix "looks obvious".
## Worktrees, runners and CI
- Make every change in a git worktree. A full test run, and each compile
  for a merge, runs on the CI runners, not on this laptop.
- Merge a worktree into a `develop` branch only after its CI run passes.
  Before the first publish that branch is `vibe` and no `main` exists;
  commits stay unsigned until a push signs them (RULES.md 16).
- Compile for a local test run: a small project (clean build 5 min or
  less) builds here; a large one builds on a runner, then copy the binary.
- Until the runners exist, ask before a large build or a full test run.
